title: How to find out who owns a company
summary: How to find out who owns a company: read its filings, SEC reports and the UK's PSC register, then follow any parent to a person. Sixtyfour runs the research.
body_markdown:
Start with the registry where the company was formed and read what it has filed, then follow the names it gives: shareholders or members for the legal owners and, through any parent company, the beneficial owner, the person who ultimately owns or controls it. For a US public company, the 10-K, the proxy statement and Schedules 13D and 13G on the SEC's EDGAR database name its officers, directors and largest holders. In the UK, Companies House publishes each company's people with significant control for free.


Not necessarily. Shareholders own a company, while directors, whom the shareholders elect, oversee its management, and the two are separate roles that one person can hold together. In a small company one person may be both, so a director's name is a lead worth checking against a shareholder record, a register of people with significant control or the company's own ownership chart.


Follow the ownership chain until it reaches a natural person. Read each layer's registry entry and filings, treat every parent company as a new search, and record the source of each link. A beneficial owner is always a person, so a chain that ends at a company, a trust or a record that names no one is unfinished, and the file should say where it stopped.


Search the company on Companies House's free Find and update company information service and open its register of people with significant control. Each entry names a person or a company and states how they control it, in bands such as more than 25 percent and up to 50 percent of the shares. The officers list and the filing history, including confirmation statements that record changes to shareholders, fill in the rest.


Search the company on the SEC's EDGAR database. Item 12 of its annual report on Form 10-K, often given in the proxy statement instead, shows the shares held by its directors, officers and certain large shareholders, and Schedules 13D and 13G report a person or group holding more than 5 percent of a voting class of its shares. Forms 3, 4 and 5 report the holdings and trades of its officers, directors and holders of more than 10 percent.


Yes. Sixtyfour is a research agent that takes a company's name or website and returns the fields you ask for, such as its officers, its parent company and the people who ultimately own it, each with its sources and, when you ask for one, a 0 to 100 confidence score. You can tell it to follow each parent company until it reaches a person, anything it could not establish is reported as open, and a person on your team decides.


Look up the trading name in the assumed-name or fictitious business name records of the county or state where the business operates. In Los Angeles County, for example, the statement lists every owner of the trading name and their residence address. If the owner listed is a company, look that company up in the state registry and follow it as you would any other.
